title: "Get started"
description: >
  From survey data to a map of disease prevalence and its uncertainty, in one
  page.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 6,
  fig.height = 5.4,
  out.width = "80%",
  fig.align = "center",
  dpi = 150
)
# The country and county boundaries are downloaded once by precompute.R, so
# that the article doesn't depend on the boundary service when it is built.
boundaries <- readRDS("precomputed/liberia-boundaries.rds")
```

This article goes from survey data to a map of prevalence in a few steps. It
fits a geostatistical model to counts of people found with a disease in a set
of villages, checks how the fit was computed, predicts prevalence across the
country with its uncertainty, and summarises it by county. The other articles
take each step further.

## The data

The `liberia` data give, for 90 villages in Liberia, the number of people
examined for the nodules of river blindness (`ntest`) and the number found with
them (`npos`).

```{r load-data, message = FALSE}
library(RiskMap)
library(sf)

data(liberia)
head(liberia)
```

RiskMap works with `sf` objects whose coordinates have a reference system. The
coordinates here are longitude and latitude, so the data are projected to the
coordinate reference system that `propose_crs()` chooses, which keeps the
distances between villages accurate.

```{r project-data}
liberia <- st_as_sf(liberia,
                    coords = c("long", "lat"),
                    crs = 4326)
crs <- propose_crs(liberia)
liberia <- st_transform(liberia, crs)
```

## Fitting the model

The model treats the number of positives in each village as binomial, and adds
a spatial Gaussian process, `gp()`, to the logit of prevalence. Nearby villages
then share part of their risk. Covariates enter the formula as in `glm()`.
Binomial models are fitted by Monte Carlo maximum likelihood, so `set.seed()`
makes the fit reproducible.

```{r fit-model}
set.seed(2026)
fit <- glgpm(npos ~ gp(),
             data = liberia,
             family = "binomial",
             denominator = ntest)
summary(fit)
```

The spatial correlation scale is the distance over which the correlation
between two villages falls by a factor of about three. With the exponential
correlation used by default, the practical range, the distance at which the
correlation falls to 0.05, is about three times the scale.

## Checking the fit

`check_fit()` goes through the checks on how the fit was computed and flags
anything that needs attention. The article *Checking a fit* covers it, with
profile likelihoods and the parametric bootstrap.

```{r check-fit}
check_fit(fit)
```

## Predicting across the country

Predictions are made on a grid of points covering Liberia, built by
`create_grid()` from the country's boundary. The boundaries come from
[geoBoundaries](https://www.geoboundaries.org/) through the geobounds package.

```{r download-boundaries, eval = FALSE}
library(geobounds)
border <- st_transform(gb_get_adm0("Liberia"), crs)
counties <- st_transform(gb_get_adm1("Liberia"), crs)
```

```{r load-boundaries, include = FALSE}
border <- boundaries$border
counties <- boundaries$counties
```

`predict()` gives the predictive distribution of prevalence at each point of
the grid. Its summaries here are the mean, the limits of a 95% interval, and
the probability that prevalence exceeds 20%.

```{r predict-grid}
grid <- create_grid(border, spacing = 5)
prediction <- predict(fit,
                      newdata = grid,
                      summaries = c("mean", "lower", "upper", "exceedance"),
                      thresholds = 0.2)
plot(prediction)
```

Every result of RiskMap has a `plot()` method, and a function with the same
arguments and its own help page, such as `plot_prediction()` for predictions.
This article uses `plot()` for a plain map and the `plot_*()` function when it
sets arguments. Here they map the limits of the 95% interval, and the
probability that prevalence exceeds 20%.

```{r plot-interval, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.4, out.width = "100%"}
plot_prediction(prediction, summaries = c("lower", "upper"))
```

```{r plot-exceedance}
plot_prediction(prediction, summaries = "exceedance", thresholds = 0.2)
```

## Summarising by county

With `boundaries`, `predict()` also averages the predictions over each area.
The draws at the grid points are then joint, so the average of each county has
a proper interval.

```{r predict-counties}
by_county <- predict(fit,
                     newdata = grid,
                     boundaries = counties,
                     aggregate = "mean")
to_table(by_county)
plot(by_county)
```

## Where next

- *Projections and distances* explains the choice of a coordinate reference
  system and the empirical variogram.
- *Families and links* fits counts, continuous outcomes and other links.
- *Checking a fit* looks closer at how a fit was computed and at the
  uncertainty of its estimates.
- *Prediction targets* covers exceedance probabilities, population weights,
  transformed targets and standardisation.
- *Assessing predictions and simulations* compares models by spatial
  cross-validation and on simulated data.

Chapters [3](https://www.mbgr.org/03_model-fitting.html) and
[4](https://www.mbgr.org/04_geostatistical-prediction.html) of the book
*Model-based geostatistics for global public health using R* treat model
fitting and prediction at length.
